subject: chemistry-hl
topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: For a reaction to occur, particles must collide with:
choices: Energy at least equal to Ea and the correct orientation
Any amount of energy, as long as they collide often
Energy greater than ΔH for the overall reaction
The correct orientation only, whatever their energy
items.note: Collision theory: successful collisions need E ≥ Ea and an appropriate geometry.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: Increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution increases the rate because:
choices: Each collision has more energy than before
The activation energy of the reaction is lowered
The particles move faster at the same temperature
Collisions between reactant particles happen more frequently
items.note: More particles per unit volume → more collisions per second. Energy per collision is unchanged.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: A catalyst increases the rate of reaction by:
choices: Increasing the kinetic energy of the reacting particles
Shifting the position of equilibrium to the products
Providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
Increasing the enthalpy change of the reaction
items.note: A catalyst lowers Ea; it is not consumed, and does not change ΔH or the equilibrium position.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: On a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, raising the temperature:
choices: Moves the peak left and raises it, with fewer particles above Ea
Moves the peak right and lowers it, with more particles above Ea
Moves Ea to the left, so more particles can react
Increases the total area under the curve
items.note: The curve flattens and shifts right; the area (number of particles) is unchanged; the fraction with E ≥ Ea increases a lot.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: Powdered marble reacts faster with acid than marble chips of the same mass because the powder has:
choices: A lower activation energy than the chips
A larger surface area, so more frequent collisions
More calcium carbonate particles in total
Particles that move faster in the acid
items.note: Same mass, more exposed surface → more collisions per second at the surface.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: Which method is suitable for following the rate of CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)?
choices: Measuring the colour change with a colorimeter
Measuring the change in pressure of a sealed liquid
Measuring the volume of the solid with a ruler
Measuring the loss of mass on a balance over time
items.note: CO₂ escapes, so mass falls with time (or collect gas in a syringe). There is no coloured species.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: The rate equation is rate = k[A]²[B]. If [A] is doubled and [B] is halved, the rate:
choices: Doubles
Quadruples
Stays the same
Halves

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: For rate = k[A][B]², what are the units of k when concentration is in mol dm⁻³ and rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹?
choices: mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹
mol² dm⁻⁶ s⁻¹
mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
s⁻¹
items.note: Overall order 3: k = rate ÷ conc³ → (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹) ÷ (mol³ dm⁻⁹) = mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: A reaction is first order in X. A graph of rate against [X] is:
choices: A straight line through the origin
A horizontal line
A curve with increasing gradient
A straight line with a negative gradient
items.note: First order: rate ∝ [X]. Zero order gives a horizontal line; second order a curve upward.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: The mechanism of a reaction is: Step 1 (slow) NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO; Step 2 (fast) NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂. The rate equation is:
choices: rate = k[NO₂][CO]
rate = k[NO₂]²
rate = k[NO₃][CO]
rate = k[NO₂]²[CO]
items.note: The rate-determining (slow) step involves two NO₂, so CO does not appear in the rate equation.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: A reaction's rate constant doubles from 300 K to 310 K. Using the Arrhenius equation, Ea is about: (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
choices: 5.4 kJ mol⁻¹
540 kJ mol⁻¹
0.54 kJ mol⁻¹
54 kJ mol⁻¹

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: Explain, using collision theory, why a 10 °C rise in temperature can roughly double the rate of many reactions.
markscheme: Particles have more kinetic energy and collide more frequently (1)
Much larger proportion of collisions have energy ≥ Ea (1)
The second effect is the main reason for the large increase (1)
items.tactic: Mention both factors, then say which dominates.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: Sketch a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution and use it to explain how a catalyst increases the rate.
markscheme: Axes: number/fraction of particles vs kinetic energy; curve starts at origin, does not meet the x-axis (1)
Catalysed Ea marked at lower energy than uncatalysed Ea (1)
Larger area beyond the catalysed Ea, so more particles have enough energy to react (1)
items.tactic: Label both Ea values on the energy axis; shade or name the area that matters.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem: Data for A + B → C: Exp 1 [A] 0.10, [B] 0.10, rate 2.0 × 10⁻⁴; Exp 2 [A] 0.20, [B] 0.10, rate 8.0 × 10⁻⁴; Exp 3 [A] 0.10, [B] 0.30, rate 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ (mol dm⁻³ and mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹). Deduce the rate equation and calculate k with units.
markscheme: Exp 1→2: [A] doubles, rate × 4, so second order in A (1)
Exp 1→3: [B] triples, rate × 3, so first order in B (1)
items.tactic: Change one concentration at a time; compare the factor in rate with the factor in concentration.

items.topicLabel: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Magnesium ribbon (0.050 g) reacted with excess HCl. Volume of H₂ (cm³) at 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 60 s: 0, 18, 31, 40, 45, 48.
(a) Calculate the mean rate over the first 20 s. (b) Describe how the rate changes and explain why. (c) Suggest why the final volume is 48 cm³ and not more. (d) Suggest one source of random error.
markscheme: (b) Rate decreases over time (18 cm³ in first 10 s, 5 cm³ from 30–40 s) (1)
Because the Mg is used up/surface area falls and acid concentration falls, so fewer collisions per second (1)
(c) Mg is the limiting reactant; all of it has reacted (1)
(d) e.g. reading the syringe/timing by eye, or ribbon length varying (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
